The blades are among the most expensive components of a wind turbine, accounting for 10-20% of total manufacturing costs.
Larger and more flexible blades have been designed to harvest more energy, but this has led to lower safety margins.
Cracks and delaminations are the most common forms of blade damage, typically occurring close to the blade root where bending strains are highest.
Blade failures can damage not only the turbine they were attached to, but also other nearby turbines.
The proposed SHM system uses SCADA data, which has a low-pass filter applied but is still capable of identifying long-term degradation in blade stiffness and edge frequency.
The Gaussian Processes are trained on a subset of the SCADA data, using the edge frequencies of one blade as outputs and the edge frequencies and ambient temperature of another blade as inputs.
The trained GPs are used to predict the edge frequencies of each blade, and the residuals between the predictions and actual frequencies are used as a damage indicator.
X-bar control charts are used to analyze the GP residuals, with averages exceeding 3σ thresholds indicating the blades are no longer in a normal condition.
The case studies showed the proposed SHM system was able to identify the early onset of blade damage up to 6 months before it was identified and remedied.
The Gaussian Process approach is more robust to the noisy and nonstationary conditions of operational wind turbines compared to simpler regression methods.
The use of X-bar control charts with 3σ thresholds is intended to balance the trade-offs between true and false positives in damage detection.
The proposed SHM methodology can also be applied to offshore wind turbines, where maintenance access is more challenging and costly.

The versatility of the Gaussian Process approach means it can learn complex nonlinear relationships between blade frequencies and environmental/operational variables without requiring predetermined functional forms.

The normalization of the data prior to the application of the machine learning methods is done to avoid numerical instabilities and to avoid disclosing confidential information about blade properties.
The selection of training data for the Gaussian Processes is done using the first two years of turbine operation, assuming the blades were in a normal condition during this period.
